editor_spans.body: The Prime Minister presents Scotland's centralisation as something Holyrood did after 1999, calling it 'the most devolved nation in the UK' yet 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe'. The cause is older, and it was decided in London. Between 1975 and 1996 Scotland had the regional tier he now wants to rebuild: Strathclyde and the other regional councils, which ran transport, strategic planning and economic development across city regions. Westminster abolished them in the mid-1990s reorganisation, three years before the Scottish Parliament existed. What was left was 32 single-tier councils, each large by European standards and none matching a functioning economic region. Holyrood inherited that map and has mostly worked around it, through City Region Deals, joint boards and national agencies, without redrawing it. When he says Scottish city regions need their own 'resources and decision-making powers', he is asking for something Scotland had a generation ago and lost through a UK decision. That matters for his offer. Rebuilding a regional tier means Holyrood legislating to rearrange local government. Asking the SNP to do that at a UK Prime Minister's suggestion is a far bigger request than the friendly framing implies.

The one concrete new item is 'DWP devolution', and it contains a tension the speech never resolves. The model he praises, Easterhouse's 'names not numbers', worked because it was voluntary and built on trust: clothes for interviews, travel paid, a pathway designed around each person. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) system it would sit inside runs on conditionality and sanctions. In the same speech he says he 'won't have a country where we get comfortable with the idea of kids in their 20s just being there on benefits', and he points to the Milburn review. That sounds like tougher expectations, not looser ones. Scotland already gained powers over some employment programmes under the 2016 Scotland Act, and the limit was always the same: Holyrood could design the support, but Westminster kept the benefit rules that decide whether a claimant trusts the adviser in front of them. If the offer devolves jobcentre-style support while Universal Credit conditions stay set in London, the 'computer says no' problem he describes will just be delivered locally. Whether it amounts to more depends on whether conditionality is also on the table at the National Economic Council, and the speech is silent on that.

His account of Ravenscraig fits his argument almost too neatly: a 'decision taken hundreds of miles away' by people who never lived with the consequences. But the works closed in 1992, four years after British Steel was privatised, and the decision came from a company boardroom, not from Whitehall. Deeper devolution of the kind he offers would not have changed that decision. The lever in his speech that would have mattered is the one he used himself as mayor: public buyers choosing to pay a little more for things made locally, like Greater Manchester's buses from Alexander Dennis in Falkirk. In a market economy, deindustrialisation is decided by owners and customers more than by governments. A reindustrialisation plan for Scotland will depend more on how procurement rules are rewritten across the UK than on how much power Holyrood passes down to the regions.
